content.title: How can a good God allow suffering?
content.summary: God is sovereign and good; evil is real, and Christ is our hope.

answer.text: God governs all things without becoming the author of sin. Scripture never asks us to call evil good. It shows him bringing good through what creatures intend for evil, supremely at Christ's cross. We know his character and promises without knowing his hidden purpose in every loss.

reasoning.text: Joseph names his brothers' intention as evil and God's intention in the same events as good.
Jesus was delivered according to God's purpose, yet those who crucified him acted wickedly.
For those who love God, suffering cannot defeat his purpose of conforming them to Christ.

conclusion.text: Our hope rests in God's sovereign goodness and the risen Christ, not in pretending we can explain every tragedy.

sections.text: Baptists confess together that God the Father “reigns with providential care” over his universe and the flow of human history, and that his perfect knowledge extends even to the future decisions of his free creatures (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article II). The Abstract of Principles (1858), the confession of the first Southern Baptist seminary, says that God “decrees or permits” all things that come to pass, yet is never the author or approver of sin and does not destroy the free will and responsibility of his creatures (article IV). Scripture holds divine purpose and creaturely responsibility together. It does not portray God as helpless before human decisions or blind natural forces.
sections.title: Where Baptists agree

sections.text: Baptists explain God's government of evil in two main ways, and the site's confession does not choose between them. Calvinist Baptists, with the Second London Confession of 1689 and Westminster before it, hold that God ordains whatever comes to pass: every evil falls within his eternal decree, while the sin belongs wholly to the creature who commits it. R. C. Sproul argues this way from Genesis 50:20. Non-Calvinist Baptists hold that God permits much that he does not cause: he made creatures with real freedom, knows every choice they will make, and weaves even their evil choices into his purpose without determining them. Some of them, called Molinists, add that God knows what every creature would freely do in any situation and governs the world by that knowledge. This free-will account does not place suffering outside God's government; that claim belongs to open theism, which the Baptist Faith and Message excludes by affirming God's knowledge of his creatures' future decisions. Both accounts confess that God is sovereign, that he is not the author of sin, and that the cross shows him bringing salvation out of the worst human evil.
sections.title: Two Baptist accounts of how God governs evil

sections.text: Jesus weeps at Lazarus's tomb. The Psalms give words for anguish. When someone is grieving, listening and weeping with them may be the first faithful response. God's promises do not require them to disguise pain.
sections.title: Lament belongs to faith

content.objection: Does a good purpose make evil acceptable?

reply.text: No. The brothers' evil remained evil, and the crucifixion involved guilty human action. God's power to redeem suffering does not authorise us to inflict, conceal or excuse it.

limit.text: Romans 8:28 is a promise to those who love God, not a claim that every event feels good. Do not announce the secret reason for someone's loss as if God had revealed it to you.

prompt.text: Would it help more to discuss the question now, or to have someone listen and grieve with you?
